title: What is a Hedge Fund?
subtitle: A flexible fund for institutions and wealthy individuals, with lighter regulation
openingQuestion: In what key way does a hedge fund differ from a mutual fund or ETF in its investment strategy?
openingOptions: A hedge fund has a lower management fee than an ETF
A hedge fund can use far more flexible strategies: high leverage, short selling, complex derivatives, illiquid assets - while mutual funds/ETFs are tightly bound by regulation
A hedge fund may only invest in bonds
explanation: A hedge fund is a private investment fund for institutional and high-net-worth ('accredited') investors, with much lighter regulation than a mutual fund/ETF. It is allowed to use a diverse range of strategies: high leverage, short selling, complex derivatives, illiquid assets - aiming to generate Alpha in any market condition (including a falling market).

realWorldExample.description: Renaissance Technologies, one of the most successful hedge funds in history, uses complex mathematical models and algorithms to trade - its internal Medallion Fund achieved outstanding average returns for decades in a row.

quiz.question: What does a hedge fund's common '2 and 20' fee structure mean?
options: A committed 2% return and a 20% annual return cap
A 2% management fee and a 20% withdrawal fee upon full redemption
A 2% annual management fee plus 20% of the excess profit
Maximum leverage of 2x and a maximum 20% weight per position
quiz.explanation: '2 and 20' is the classic fee structure: a 2% annual asset management fee regardless of performance, plus 20% of the excess profit generated (usually above a hurdle rate). This structure aligns the fund manager's interest with actual performance, but also makes the overall cost to investors much higher than an ordinary ETF/mutual fund.

quiz.question: Why do hedge funds often require investors to commit to a lock-up period, rather than allowing free withdrawal at any time?
options: So the fund has time to collect its full committed management fee
So investors can't withdraw while the fund sits on a deep unrealized loss
Because regulation requires every private fund to have a lock-up
To avoid being forced to sell illiquid assets at a fire-sale price when redemptions hit
quiz.explanation: A lock-up period protects both the fund and remaining investors from being forced to sell illiquid assets at an unfavorable price to meet sudden redemption demands - a trade-off between liquidity and the ability to pursue more complex, longer-term strategies.

quiz.question: A fund returns 15% for the year. Under the 2-and-20 structure, how much does the investor actually receive?
options: About 10.4% (= (15% − 2%) × 0.8 after the performance fee)
About 13% (= 15% − 2%, deducting only the management fee)
About 12% (= 15% − 20% × 15%, deducting only the performance fee)
Exactly 15%, because fees are already included in the reported return
quiz.explanation: Subtracting the 2% management fee leaves 13%; 20% of that is a 2.6% performance fee, leaving 10.4%. Nearly a third of the return went to fees - one reason this structure has drawn growing criticism.

quiz.question: What does a high-water mark in a hedge fund contract do?
options: Guarantees the investor cannot lose more than a predefined threshold
Prevents the fund from charging a performance fee twice on a gain that merely offsets an earlier loss
Caps the maximum leverage the fund is allowed to use
Sets a minimum asset value for the fund to keep operating
quiz.explanation: A fund that loses 20% and then gains 20% back still has not returned to its old level, so no performance fee is due yet. Without this clause, a fund oscillating near break-even would still collect a fee every year it happens to be up.

quiz.question: Why is average hedge fund industry performance often rated higher than it actually is?
options: Because the performance fee is added back into reported returns
Because hedge funds are allowed to publish unaudited performance figures to their investors
Because funds that shut down from losses drop out of the statistical data
Because only the largest funds have to report to regulators
quiz.explanation: This is survivorship bias: a fund that collapses stops reporting, so the rankings only reflect those that remain. Studies show adjusting for this bias pulls the industry's average return down significantly.

keyTakeaways: Hedge fund: a flexible private fund, less bound by regulation than a mutual fund/ETF
Can use high leverage, short selling, and complex derivatives to generate Alpha
The typical '2 and 20' fee structure makes it far more expensive than a passive fund

practicePrompt.question: A fund only accepts capital from institutions and wealthy individuals (not open to the general public), and is free to use high leverage, short selling, and complex derivative strategies that an ordinary mutual fund is not allowed to use. What is this type of fund called?
options: This is called a Mutual Fund, a type of open fund available to the general investing public
Hedge fund: a flexible private fund, less bound by regulation than a mutual fund
This is called an ETF, a type of fund that trades flexibly like a stock on the exchange
This type of fund does not exist in practice, it is only a theoretical concept in finance
practicePrompt.explanation: Hedge fund: a flexible private fund, less bound by regulation than a mutual fund/ETF. It can use high leverage, short selling, and complex derivatives to generate Alpha, but its fee structure is usually high ('2 and 20') and it is only open to qualified investors.

application.title: Understand the 2-and-20 fee structure
application.message: Try calculating: if a hedge fund manages VND 1 billion for you with a '2 and 20' fee, how much fixed management fee and performance fee would you pay if the fund gains 20% for the year.
application.secondary: This figure helps you see why a hedge fund needs a very large Alpha to genuinely be worth investing in.

sections.text: A hedge fund is a private investment fund for institutional and high-net-worth ('accredited') investors, with much lighter regulation than a mutual fund or ETF. A hedge fund is allowed to use a diverse range of strategies - high leverage, short selling, complex derivatives, illiquid assets - aiming to generate Alpha in any market condition, including a falling market.

'2 and 20' is the hedge fund's classic fee structure: a 2% annual asset management fee regardless of performance, plus 20% of the excess profit generated (performance fee), usually above a hurdle rate. This structure aligns the manager's interest with actual performance, but also makes the overall cost to investors much higher than an ordinary ETF or mutual fund. Renaissance Technologies, using mathematical models and algorithms to trade, is one of the most successful hedge funds in history.
Why there is a lock-up period

Many hedge fund strategies invest in illiquid assets or need a long time to realize gains. If free withdrawal were allowed at any time, the fund could be forced to sell assets at an unfavorable moment to meet a sudden redemption request, affecting remaining investors. A lock-up period is the trade-off between liquidity and the ability to pursue more complex, longer-term investment strategies.
